explainBack.question: Why does having every prediction precomputed in the Atlas speed up research, and why can a top-ranked score still not tell a patient what their DNA change means for them?
explainBack.answer: Before the Atlas, a lab facing hundreds of candidate variants had to run the model's prediction for each one; now the answers for all roughly nine billion single-letter changes are already computed and can simply be looked up, so the slow step of generating predictions disappears and researchers jump straight to ranking which changes might matter. But the score only predicts a molecular effect — for example, that a change could alter how cells splice a gene message. Whether that effect really happens must be shown in an experiment, as with the epilepsy case where lab-grown cells confirmed some changes produced the longer message. And even a confirmed molecular effect is only one link in the evidence chain for a diagnosis, which also needs clinical context the score cannot supply.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: An accurate answer must include: lookup replaces per-variant computation (P002), the score's role is prioritization not proof (P003, P007), the lab check as the verifying step (P004), and the report's own statement that predictions are only part of the clinical evidence chain (P005).
explainBack.assessment: The article supports this answer fully; every element of the causal chain is present in P002–P005 in ordinary language, so a reader can reconstruct both the speed-up and the diagnosis boundary without outside knowledge.

unseenTransfer.scenario: A cardiology research group studies a family with unexplained inherited heart-rhythm problems. Genome sequencing yields 400 DNA variants shared by affected relatives, most in non-coding regions, and the group has budget to laboratory-test only a handful.
unseenTransfer.question: Using the article's mechanism, how should the group use the Atlas, and what may they conclude — and not conclude — from a variant that the Atlas ranks first?
unseenTransfer.answer: They should look up the precomputed predictions for all 400 variants instead of computing each afresh, and use the rankings to shortlist the few candidates predicted to disturb molecular function in heart-relevant contexts. A top-ranked variant is a research lead: the next step is an experiment, such as testing the surrounding DNA stretch in laboratory-grown heart cells to see whether the predicted molecular change actually occurs. Even if the experiment confirms it, they cannot tell family members that this variant is their diagnosis — a confirmed molecular effect is only part of the clinical evidence chain, and clinical genetics evaluation would still be needed before it could inform anyone's care.
